patterns.name: Prompted foundation model
patterns.summary: A hosted foundation model with engineered system prompts, structured output and guardrails. No custom retrieval or training.
patterns.whenToUse: General drafting, summarizing content the user supplies, or extraction where the input contains everything the model needs.
patterns.watchOut: Answers about your organization will be invented if the model is not given your data. Treat it as a starting pattern, not a knowledge system.

patterns.name: Retrieval augmented generation (RAG)
patterns.summary: Index your content, retrieve the most relevant passages for each request, and have the model answer only from those passages with citations.
patterns.whenToUse: Questions over policies, documentation, tickets or any content that changes and must be cited.
patterns.watchOut: Most RAG failures are retrieval failures. Budget time for chunking, metadata, hybrid search and permission trimming before tuning prompts.

patterns.name: Tool-using agent
patterns.summary: A model that plans and calls tools (APIs, MCP servers, functions) to complete tasks, usually with retrieval for grounding.
patterns.whenToUse: The solution must read from or write to business systems, or complete multi-step work rather than only answer.
patterns.watchOut: Excessive agency is the top production risk. Scope every tool, give the agent its own identity, and require approval for writes until evaluation proves otherwise.

patterns.name: Orchestrated multi-agent system
patterns.summary: Several specialised agents coordinated by an orchestrator or workflow, often across teams or platforms using protocols such as MCP and A2A.
patterns.whenToUse: Distinct sub-tasks need different tools, permissions or owners, and a single agent's prompt and toolset has become unmanageable.
patterns.watchOut: Cost, latency and failure modes multiply with every hop. Start with one agent and split only when evaluation shows a clear gain.

patterns.name: Fine-tuned or distilled model
patterns.summary: Adapt a base model on curated examples to lock in format, tone, domain vocabulary or to run a smaller, cheaper model at scale.
patterns.whenToUse: Prompting and retrieval are proven but you need consistent style, lower latency or lower unit cost at high volume.
patterns.watchOut: Fine-tuning does not teach reliable facts. Keep retrieval for knowledge, and plan to retrain whenever the base model is retired.

patterns.name: Predictive machine learning
patterns.summary: Supervised or unsupervised models trained on structured historical data, served behind an API with drift monitoring.
patterns.whenToUse: Forecasting, scoring, anomaly detection and classification on tabular or time series data.
patterns.watchOut: Generative AI is rarely the right tool for numeric prediction. Use it for explanation on top of a predictive model, not instead of one.

riskTiers.name: Minimal
riskTiers.description: Internal, low-impact assistance on non-sensitive data. Standard engineering controls apply.

riskTiers.name: Limited
riskTiers.description: Users interact with AI directly or sensitive data is involved. Transparency, privacy and safety controls are required.

riskTiers.name: High
riskTiers.description: The system acts in business systems, handles regulated data, or influences decisions about people. Human oversight, formal evaluation and risk sign-off are required.

riskTiers.name: Restricted review
riskTiers.description: Likely in a regulated high-risk category. Legal, privacy and risk teams must review before any pilot with real users.

controls.title: Register the solution in the AI inventory with an accountable owner
Use managed or federated identities; no API keys in code
Route all model calls through a gateway with quotas, rate limits and per-team cost attribution
Set hard spend caps and alerts per environment and per consumer
Emit OpenTelemetry GenAI traces for prompts, tool calls, tokens and latency
Apply prompt injection detection on user input and retrieved content
Validate and encode model output before it reaches other systems or browsers
Keep secrets and authorization logic out of system prompts
Tell users they are interacting with AI and label generated content
Enable content safety filters for harmful content in input and output
Detect and redact personal data in prompts, logs and training sets
Complete a privacy impact assessment (DPIA) before pilot
Pin model and data processing to approved regions; confirm no cross-region inference
Enforce source permissions at retrieval time (security trimming)
Require citations and run groundedness checks on answers
Control who can add content to the index; scan sources for poisoning
Give each agent its own identity with least-privilege, scoped tool permissions
Require human approval for write or irreversible actions
Provide a kill switch and per-agent action rate limits
Allow-list MCP servers and tools; review tool descriptions as untrusted input
Pin model versions and track model retirement dates
Document training data lineage, consent and licensing
Test for bias across relevant groups and document results
Run adversarial red teaming before production and after major changes
Define human oversight: who reviews, when they intervene, how users contest outcomes
Retain tamper-evident logs of inputs, outputs, tool calls and approvals
Obtain formal risk acceptance from risk, legal and the business owner
Maintain technical documentation and a model or system card
Have legal confirm the regulatory classification (for example EU AI Act high-risk) before pilot
Add AI-specific incident runbooks (harmful output, data leak, runaway cost, rogue agent)
Monitor data and prediction drift with retraining triggers
